name: Henbane hair dye

lead: Henbane hair dye refers to the historical use of black henbane (Hyoscyamus niger) in recipes for colouring hair black. It appears in accounts of the medieval cosmetic writings attributed to Trotula of Salerno.
The appearance goal was darker hair. Secondary sources say the same cosmetic writings list other plants, such as saffron and madder, for lighter or golden shades.

paras: The sources consulted do not describe how henbane was prepared or applied. Extracts of the listed plants were reportedly often mixed with liquorice and used as shampoo.

Black henbane contains hyoscyamine and scopolamine. Reviews describe poisoning with dilated pupils, fast heart rate, agitation, convulsions and coma. It is a prescription-only material in most Western countries.

chain: Historical recipe aimed at black colour
angle.text: Medieval cosmetic recipes are said to have used henbane to colour hair black. Whether it dyed hair effectively has not been studied, and the plant's toxicity makes it a historical curiosity.

lead: Henbane hair dye is a historical cosmetic practice in which black henbane, a toxic nightshade-family plant, was recommended to colour hair black. Accounts of medieval cosmetics credit Trotula of Salerno's writings on women's adornment with the recipe, listing henbane or sage for black.[1]

The same sources list other plants for lighter shades: agrimony and boxwood for blond, and saffron, madder and celandine among golden tones. Such recipes were repeated in 15th-century cosmetic handbooks.[1] Scholarly dating and authorship of the Trotula-related texts varies, and some are described as 13th-century Anglo-Norman works.[2]

Henbane is better known as a medicinal and poisonous plant. Reviews report that all parts contain tropane alkaloids including hyoscyamine and scopolamine, and that poisoning can cause tachycardia, agitation, convulsions and coma.[3] No studies have tested it as a hair colourant.

paras: A medieval-history site summarising the Trotula cosmetics says black henbane or sage was used for colouring hair black, and does not describe preparation or safety.[1] The Trotula name covers several texts, and one Anglo-Norman cosmetic work, Ornatus mulierum, is dated to the thirteenth century.[2]

A descriptive review states that henbane leaves, seeds and roots contain alkaloids and that acute poisoning produces mydriasis, tachycardia, arrhythmia, agitation, convulsion and coma.[3] The plant has long been used medicinally and is sold only by prescription in most Western countries.[4]

timeline.event: Trotula-attributed cosmetic texts record hair-colouring recipes, including henbane for black.[1][2]
